analysis.one_liner: Multiplies public matching funds for small presidential donations while curbing big checks and lobbyist bundling.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in October 2017 by Senator Tom Udall with zero cosponsors, never got a hearing or vote before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rebuild the presidential public financing system. Candidates who agree to cap donations at $1,000 per person and refuse lobbyist-bundled money would receive a 600% federal match on small contributions, up to $300 million. It would also force presidential campaigns to disclose who bundles money for them, bar candidates from joining joint fundraising committees that collect six-figure checks, repeal the special high-limit accounts national parties use, and cap what any person can give to super PAC-style groups at $5,000 a year.
analysis.who_benefits: Presidential candidates who rely on small donors would get $6 in public funds for every $1 from a contributor giving $200 or less, up to $300 million, letting them run competitive campaigns without courting large donors. Small-dollar contributors would see their money multiplied, and voters would get new disclosure of who bundles campaign cash.

how_it_helps.text: Candidates in the public system would receive 600% matching payments on individual contributions of $200 or less, with total payments capped at $300 million and adjusted for inflation after 2019.
To qualify, candidates must refuse contributions over $1,000 per person and refuse bundled contributions forwarded by lobbyists and others covered by the bundling rules.
Presidential campaigns would have to file a separate schedule naming anyone who bundles more than $50,000 in contributions, with their employer, so voters can see who is raising money for whom.
Candidates would be barred from participating in joint fundraising committees, the vehicles used to solicit large checks from a single donor to several committees at once.

Contributions to political committees that make only independent expenditures — the super PAC model — would be capped at $5,000 per person per year, and the special high-limit accounts at national party committees would be repealed, with existing balances refunded to contributors.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers fund the expanded program through the Presidential Election Campaign Fund, fed by the voluntary income-tax checkoff; the bill authorizes Treasury advances to the fund because receipts may not cover the new payments. Large donors, lobbyists, and super PACs lose fundraising avenues.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers via the public campaign fund

drawbacks.text: Participating candidates could each draw up to $300 million in public matching payments, with automatic inflation increases after 2019, so the program's cost to the federal fund would be substantial.
The bill repeals presidential spending limits while expanding public payments, meaning total campaign spending could keep rising even as taxpayer money flows in.
The fund is financed by a voluntary tax checkoff whose receipts may fall short, which is why the bill authorizes the Treasury to make repayable advances to the fund for the first cycle.

The $5,000 cap on giving to independent-expenditure committees would sharply restrict super PACs and would almost certainly face a First Amendment challenge; the bill builds in expedited court review anticipating exactly such challenges.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is straightforward: a few hundred million dollars per election cycle in public campaign money, in exchange for making $200 donors matter as much as $2,700 donors and cutting lobbyists and super PAC money out of participating campaigns. The weak points are the cost to the fund, the removal of spending limits, and the legal risk around the super PAC cap. On balance the design directly targets the mechanisms that concentrate influence — large checks, bundling, and outside committees.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in the Senate in October 2017, referred to the Rules and Administration Committee, and never heard from again — no hearing, no markup, no vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Udall introduced the Empower Act of 2017 on October 5, 2017; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Rules and Administration the same day.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor.
That referral was the last action of any kind; the bill never received a committee hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large donors, lobbyist bundlers, super PACs, and national party committees are better off because the bill died: the campaign-money system as it existed stayed untouched, and no candidate had to choose between its caps and its public funds.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large donors, bundlers, and super PACs

for.name: Sen. Tom Udall
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to committee; no senator joined as a cosponsor.

against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on October 5, 2017 and took no further action; it died in committee.

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill during the two years remaining in the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no senator from either party cosponsored, so the record shows a single Democratic sponsor and no visible support or opposition to measure.

industries.note: Candidates in the public system could not accept bundled contributions forwarded by lobbyists, and presidential campaigns would have to publicly name anyone bundling over $50,000. Both rules shrink the leverage bundlers sell to their clients.

Participating candidates could accept no more than $1,000 from any person, and could no longer join joint fundraising committees built to collect six-figure checks. Donors who write the biggest checks would lose the ability to buy outsized access.

industries.industry: Super PACs and other independent-expenditure committees
industries.note: The bill caps what any individual can contribute to a committee making only independent expenditures at $5,000 per year, cutting off the mega-donor money super PACs run on.

They would lose the special high-limit accounts created in 2014 — existing balances would be refunded to contributors — but gain a raised $100 million limit on coordinated presidential spending plus inflation increases.
Every $200-or-less contribution to a participating candidate would be multiplied six-fold by public matching funds, making small givers the financial backbone of campaigns instead of an afterthought.
